factors.title: Start With Load
factors.text: Map your route, season, water needs, layers, snacks, and safety kit before looking at pack volume.

factors.title: Fit Comes First
factors.text: Prioritize torso fit, shoulder strap shape, and whether the hipbelt transfers load or simply stabilizes.

factors.title: Match the Weather
factors.text: Look for durable fabrics, protected zippers, water-resistant coatings, and realistic pack-cover compatibility.

sections.heading: Buying Factors
body: Choose a daypack by mapping your route, season, water needs, layers, and safety kit. The best pack is not the biggest or lightest one; it is the one that carries your real load without wasted bulk.

sections.heading: Capacity Guidance
body: Most hikers land between 20 and 28 liters for three-season day hikes. Move smaller only when your kit is dialed, and move larger when weather, camera gear, family gear, or long water carries make the extra space useful.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
body: Common mistakes include buying too much volume, ignoring torso fit, choosing fashion pockets over trail access, and forgetting that water weight changes carry comfort quickly.

specRows: Hydration sleeve, hipbelt pockets, compression, weather-resistant fabric

faqs.question: Is a 22-liter daypack big enough?
faqs.answer: For many three-season day hikes, yes. Cold weather, camera gear, or family carry duties may require more volume.

faqs.question: Do I need a hipbelt?
faqs.answer: A real hipbelt helps with heavier loads. Minimal waist straps mostly stabilize the pack.

faqs.question: Is this guide based on field testing?
faqs.answer: This is a research-based buying guide. It focuses on specifications, fit principles, category comparison, and practical buying factors rather than claiming hands-on field testing.
